passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Ephesus write: These are the words of Him who holds the seven stars in His right hand and walks among the seven golden lampstands. I know your deeds, your labor, and your perseverance. I know that you cannot tolerate those who are evil, and you have tested and exposed as liars those who falsely claim to be apostles. Without growing weary, you have persevered and endured many things for the sake of My name” (verses 1-3).

“But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love. Therefore, keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first. But if you do not repent, I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place” (verses 4-5).

“But you have this to your credit: You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Each of the seven messages follows a pattern. It is addressed to the church's ‘angel’. It opens with a title of Christ drawn from chapter 1. Then ‘I know’, followed by praise, and in most a rebuke: ‘But I have this against you.’ Then a call to repent, a warning, a promise ‘to the one who overcomes’, and the refrain, ‘He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’ The refrain shows that every church was meant to hear every message.

Ephesus was the greatest city of the province of Asia, a port and one of the largest cities in the eastern half of the empire. It was famous for its temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and it also had temples for the worship of the emperors. Paul had worked there for more than two years (Acts 19), and Christian tradition later linked John with the city.

Christ praises this church a great deal. It works hard. It endures. It does not put up with evil. It tests people who claim to be apostles and exposes the false ones. It has suffered for his name and not given up.

‘But I have this against you: You have abandoned your first love.’ A church can be right about doctrine and lose love: love for Christ, love for one another, or both. And without love, its lampstand can be removed. The church would stop being a light in its city.

Some commentators connect that warning with the city's harbour, which was slowly silting up, a threat to its life over time. Whether or not John's hearers caught that echo, the warning was clear.

The promise is the tree of life, lost in Eden. To those who overcome, Christ gives back what was lost at the beginning.
passages.ot:
The tree of life stood in Eden: “in the middle of the garden were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Genesis 2:9). After the fall the way to it was closed (Genesis 3:22-24). Revelation ends with it standing again by the river of the city (22:2).

And the prophets remembered Israel's first love for God: “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 2:2).
passages.hard:
Who were the Nicolaitans?

They are named twice, here and in the message to Pergamum (verse 15), and nowhere else in the Bible. Around AD 180 Irenaeus linked them with Nicolas, one of the seven chosen in Acts 6:5, but that link is uncertain, and many scholars doubt it. The text tells us only that Christ hated their works, and, in verse 15, that their teaching was held by some at Pergamum alongside the teaching of Balaam. More than that is not known, and these notes do not guess.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have been right about many things and lost your first love. Ask what ‘the deeds you did at first’ were, when your faith was new. And ask what it would mean to return to them.

passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of the First and the Last, who died and returned to life. I know your affliction and your poverty—though you are rich! And I am aware of the slander of those who falsely claim to be Jews, but are in fact a synagogue of Satan” (verses 8-9).

“Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Look, the devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you, and you will suffer tribulation for ten days. Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. The one who overcomes will not be harmed by the second death” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Smyrna was a rich port north of Ephesus, known for its loyalty to Rome. It built a temple to the goddess Roma as early as 195 BC, and in AD 26 it won the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius. Its old city had been destroyed around 600 BC and lay in ruins for centuries before it was founded again. Some hear that history in Christ's title here: ‘the First and the Last, who died and returned to life’.

The church there was poor and under pressure. Christ says, ‘I know your affliction and your poverty’, and then, ‘though you are rich’. By his account, they had what mattered.

He names their trouble. They faced slander from some in the city's synagogue (see below). And worse was coming: prison, and ‘tribulation for ten days’. In this book ten can stand for a limited fullness: a real trial, with an end set by God.

Christ does not promise to stop the suffering. He says, ‘Do not fear.’ And he gives a promise. ‘Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.’ The word for crown is the wreath given to winners at the games, and Smyrna was proud of its games and its civic wreaths. Christ promises a wreath no city could give.

Smyrna receives no rebuke at all, only comfort. Later, in the middle of the second century, its bishop Polycarp was burned to death there for refusing to deny Christ.
passages.ot:
‘Do not fear’ is God's word to Israel in trouble: “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you” (Isaiah 41:10).

A short, limited test of ten days recalls Daniel and his friends, who asked, “Please test your servants for ten days” (Daniel 1:12), and were kept faithful in a foreign court.

‘The First and the Last’ is God's own title in Isaiah: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6).
passages.hard:
What does ‘a synagogue of Satan’ mean? Has this phrase been used against Jewish people?

It must be read with great care. It is not a statement about the Jewish people. John himself was a Jew. The book is full of Israel's Scriptures from beginning to end, and the new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes of Israel (21:12). The phrase speaks of a local conflict in one city, Smyrna, in the first century, among people who all claimed to be heirs of Israel's God. Some members of the synagogue there were slandering the Christians, perhaps denouncing them to the Roman authorities, at a time when Christians were being pushed out of the legal protection that Judaism had. John's charge is that in joining in persecution they were acting as the accuser, which is what the name ‘Satan’ means, and so were not living as faithful Israel. Paul uses similar inside language: “a man is a Jew because he is one inwardly” (Romans 2:29). It is the language of a family quarrel, not a verdict on a people.

It is also true that phrases like this were later torn from their setting and used by Christians to justify contempt and violence against Jews. That reading is false. This site rejects it, and the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. Nothing in this verse says anything about Jewish people as a whole, then or now. Reading it faithfully means reading it as the first hearers did: as a word about particular accusers in one city, in one time.
passages.asks: Ask what Christ's ‘though you are rich’ means for how you measure your own life. Ask what you are afraid of suffering, and hear ‘Do not fear’. And ask whether you have ever heard a verse like this one used against Jewish people, and how you would answer it now.

passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Pergamum write: These are the words of the One who holds the sharp, double-edged sword. I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits. Yet you have held fast to My name and have not denied your faith in Me, even in the day when My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you, where Satan dwells” (verses 12-13).

“But I have a few things against you, because some of you hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality. In the same way, some of you also hold to the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Therefore repent! Otherwise I will come to you shortly and wage war against them with the sword of My mouth” (verses 14-16).

“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Pergamum, inland to the north, had been the capital of a line of kings, the last of whom left his kingdom to Rome in 133 BC. Its hill held a great altar of Zeus and temples to many gods. It had a famous healing shrine of the god Asclepius. And in 29 BC it received the first temple in the province to the emperor Augustus and the goddess Roma.

Christ says, ‘I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits.’ He knows how hard their city is. And he praises them: they have held on, even when Antipas, ‘My faithful witness’, was killed among them.

But some in the church were holding to ‘the teaching of Balaam’. In Numbers, Balaam was remembered for leading Israel into idolatry and sexual sin at Peor. In Pergamum, the same pull came through ordinary life. Trade guilds held banquets in honour of their patron gods, where meat sacrificed to idols was served, and some ancient writers linked such feasts with drunkenness and sexual licence. A Christian craftsman who refused to go could lose his business. The ‘teaching of Balaam’ likely offered a way to stay in that world by calling such things harmless.

Christ comes with ‘the sword of My mouth’. In a city where the Roman governor had the power of the sword, life and death, Christ's word outranks Rome's.

The promises: ‘hidden manna’, the bread of heaven, instead of the meat of idol feasts; and ‘a white stone inscribed with a new name’. White stones were used as votes to acquit in courts, and as tokens to enter feasts. Either picture could fit: acquitted by Christ, and welcomed to his table.
passages.ot:
Balaam's story is in Numbers. Israel at Shittim “began to indulge in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab, who also invited them to the sacrifices for their gods” (Numbers 25:1-2). Later Moses said that these women caused Israel, “through the counsel of Balaam, to turn unfaithfully against the LORD at Peor” (Numbers 31:16).

The hidden manna recalls the wilderness: “Now the house of Israel called the bread manna” (Exodus 16:31).

And the new name is Isaiah's promise: “You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow” (Isaiah 62:2).
passages.hard:
What is ‘the throne of Satan’ at Pergamum?

Readers have explained it in several ways. Some point to the great altar of Zeus on the city's hill. Some point to the serpent that was the sign of Asclepius, whose healing shrine was famous there. Some point to the city's place as a centre of emperor worship, with the first temple in the province to Augustus and Roma. Others point to the fact that the Roman governor held court there, with power over life and death. The text does not say which, and more than one may be in view. These notes do not choose.

What is clear is that Christ knew how hard it was to be faithful there, and honoured those who were.
passages.asks: Ask where you live, and what makes faithfulness hard there. Ask whether there is a ‘small accommodation’ to the idols of your world that you have called harmless. And ask what it would mean to you to be given a new name by Christ.

passages.t: Thyatira: love that grows, and a false prophetess
passages.happening:
“To the angel of the church in Thyatira write: These are the words of the Son of God, whose eyes are like a blazing fire and whose feet are like polished bronze. I know your deeds—your love, your faith, your service, your perseverance—and your latter deeds are greater than your first” (verses 18-19).

“But I have this against you: You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols. Even though I have given her time to repent of her immorality, she is unwilling. Behold, I will cast her onto a bed of sickness, and those who commit adultery with her will suffer great tribulation unless they repent of her deeds. Then I will strike her children dead, and all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts, and I will repay each of you according to your deeds” (verses 20-23).

“But I say to the rest of you in Thyatira, who do not hold to her teaching and have not learned the so-called deep things of Satan: I will place no further burden upon you. Nevertheless, hold fast to what you have until I come. And to the one who overcomes and continues in My work until the end, I will give authority over the nations. He will rule them with an iron scepter and shatter them like pottery—just as I have received authority from My Father. And I will give him the morning star. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (verses 24-29).
passages.hearers:
Thyatira, southeast of Pergamum, was a smaller trading town with many trade guilds: wool workers, dyers, leather workers, bronze smiths. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met at Philippi, came from there (Acts 16:14).

Christ comes as ‘the Son of God’ with eyes like fire. He sees everything. And what he sees first is good. This church is growing. Its love, faith, service and endurance are greater now than at the start. Ephesus had lost its first love; Thyatira's love was growing.

But it tolerated a false teacher. Christ calls her ‘Jezebel’, the name of Ahab's queen, who led Israel into the worship of Baal. This woman called herself a prophetess and taught believers that taking part in the idol feasts and the sexual sin that went with them did not matter. Some claimed to know ‘the deep things’; Christ calls them ‘the so-called deep things of Satan’.

Notice that even she was given time to repent (verse 21). Christ's judgment comes after patience refused. His words of judgment are severe (see below), and the reason he gives is that ‘all the churches will know that I am the One who searches minds and hearts’.

To the rest he lays no new burden. ‘Hold fast to what you have until I come.’ And the promise is to share his own rule, in the words of Psalm 2, and ‘the morning star’, which Revelation later uses of Christ himself (22:16).
passages.ot:
Jezebel was Ahab's queen: “Surely there was never one like Ahab, who sold himself to do evil in the sight of the LORD, incited by his wife Jezebel” (1 Kings 21:25).

The one who searches minds and hearts is the LORD of Jeremiah: “I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind to reward a man according to his way” (Jeremiah 17:10).

And the rule over the nations is the psalm of the king: “Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession. You will break them with an iron scepter” (Psalm 2:8-9).
passages.hard:
Who was ‘Jezebel’? And what do the hard words of verses 22 and 23 mean?

The text tells us that she was a woman in the church at Thyatira who called herself a prophetess, and that she taught believers to take part in idol feasts and sexual sin. ‘Jezebel’ is almost certainly not her real name. It is Christ's name for her, drawn from Ahab's queen, who led Israel into idolatry. Beyond that, nothing is known about her, and these notes do not guess.

‘Jezebel’ is not a label for any woman or any group today. The name in this passage describes one false teacher in one first-century church, and what she taught. It gives no one leave to call a woman ‘Jezebel’, for her gifts, her leadership, her dress, her opinions or anything else.

The words of judgment in verses 22 and 23 are hard. They are spoken about one teacher who was given time to repent and refused, and about those who joined in her teaching unless they repented. They are not a rule for reading anyone's illness or loss. The Bible does not teach that every sickness is a punishment for sin; Jesus refused that reasoning (John 9:3).

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether your love and service are growing, as Thyatira's were. Ask whether you have put up with a teaching that makes sin seem harmless. And ask whether you have ever heard ‘Jezebel’ used as a weapon, and what Christ's own words here say about that.
